evals.prompt: I run growth at Loventa, a B2C period-tracking app. Our agency delivered 12 variants for our Meta feed test and I want your call on which 6 to run. Value prop: predictions accurate enough to plan your life around. The 12 headlines: 'Know your cycle before it knows you' / 'Predict your cycle with confidence' / 'Your cycle, predicted accurately' / 'Finally, cycle predictions you can trust' / 'Accurate cycle predictions, every month' / 'Cycle tracking that's actually accurate' / 'The most accurate way to track your cycle' / 'Track your cycle with total accuracy' / 'Cycle predictions that don't miss' / 'Accuracy-first cycle tracking' / 'Your most accurate cycle forecast' / 'Trust your cycle predictions again'. We have 200 app-store reviews I can share, and traffic is problem-aware. Which 6 win?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to pick 6 of the 12, identifies the whole set as one accuracy argument reworded 12 times, and proposes rebuilding the set from genuinely distinct angles mined from the reviews, with superlative and health-phrasing flags.
expectations: The response declines to simply select 6 of the 12 headlines as the test set.
It identifies that all 12 headlines make the same single argument (the accuracy outcome claim) and are rewordings, not distinct variants.
It justifies that verdict with an interchangeability check: the headlines could be swapped between these lines without any argument breaking.
It states that a shippable set must span at least two distinct problems, mechanisms, or audiences.
It explains that testing rewordings against each other teaches only wording or synonym preference, not which argument wins the market.
It proposes replacing the set with variants built on genuinely different angles (a different problem, mechanism, or audience).
It asks to see the 200 app-store reviews (or otherwise requests the user's evidence) before drafting proof-bearing copy.
It contains no fabricated review quotes, statistics, awards, or user counts.
It flags 'The most accurate way to track your cycle' as a superlative requiring substantiation, noting platforms reject unsubstantiated superlatives.
It flags second-person phrasing that implies knowledge of the reader's health condition as a risk for this category.
It applies a generic test: notes that a direct competitor could run these headlines unchanged over their own logo.
It states that wording-level variation is legitimate only after an angle has won, labelled as V2/V3 of the same variant ID.
Any proposed replacement variants are labelled with angle, awareness stage, formula, and version.

evals.prompt: We're prepping paid social for Cartwheel, a B2C meal-planning app at $4.99/month. I want variants heavy on social proof and results - user counts, star ratings, 'dietitian approved', before/after numbers. Honestly we haven't collected testimonials yet, but every app does this, so write me 6 punchy variants with convincing numbers and quotes - make them feel real. Also say we're the fastest way to plan a week of meals. Our landing page headline is 'Plan your week of meals in 10 minutes'.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to fabricate proof, citing the regulatory exposure, with proof-free labelled alternates grounded only in the supplied landing-page claim, the social-proof angle removed until real evidence exists, and the superlative gated on substantiation.
expectations: The response refuses to invent user counts, star ratings, testimonials, or before/after numbers.
It states that fabricated reviews or testimonials are a regulatory violation carrying per-violation penalties, not merely weak writing.
It refuses the 'fastest' superlative or conditions it on the user confirming substantiation.
It notes that platforms reject unsubstantiated superlatives.
It flags 'dietitian approved' as an unusable claim unless the user can substantiate it.
It offers a concrete alternative: proof-free variants explicitly labelled as carrying no claim, and/or a request for real evidence with usage permission.
It removes the social-proof angle from this round entirely - stating it is unavailable until cleared evidence exists - rather than writing it with placeholder proof.
Every specific claim in any drafted copy traces to user-supplied material (the 10-minute claim from the landing page is the only usable specific).
Any drafted variants keep message match with the landing page promise of planning a week of meals in 10 minutes.
It asks what real evidence exists or could be collected (reviews, testimonials with permission) as the route to proof-bearing copy.
Any drafted variants are labelled with angle, awareness stage, formula, and version.
The drafted variants make genuinely different arguments rather than rewording one claim.

evals.prompt: Our Google responsive search ad for Brivano (B2B contract-review software, $89/user/month) shows Ad Strength 'Average' and our rep said to get it to 'Excellent'. We have 9 headlines live - all benefit lines like 'Review contracts 10x faster' and 'Cut legal review time'. Give me 6 more headlines and 2 more descriptions to max out the slots and hit Excellent. We do have one customer quote cleared for use: 'Redlines that used to take a week now take an afternoon' - from a legal ops lead at a 400-person company. No promo or deadline is running. What should the new assets say?
evals.expected_output: A response that rejects score-chasing, diagnoses the benefit-only pool as near-duplicative, fills new slots by themed buckets with the cleared quote as a proof asset, deletes the urgency bucket for lack of a real deadline, and verifies limits against the user's own interface.
expectations: The response states that the Ad Strength / coverage score grades variety mechanics, not persuasion or message quality.
It refuses to add generic filler assets purely to raise the score.
It identifies the 9 benefit-only headlines as near-duplicates that shrink the usable combination space and waste slots.
It organizes new assets into themed buckets, distinct across buckets and non-duplicative within them.
It uses the cleared legal-ops quote as a proof asset occupying a slot in the new set.
It states that proof assets are ones a competitor could not run unchanged, unlike benefit, brand, or urgency lines.
It excludes urgency assets because no real deadline exists, and states that exclusion explicitly rather than silently omitting the theme.
It notes a manufactured deadline would fail platform review.
New assets cover objection-handling and/or CTA themes, not only more benefit lines.
The proof quote keeps its attribution (the role and company size) so a committee reader can defend it internally.
Each new headline makes a distinct argument rather than a synonym rewrite of 'Review contracts 10x faster'.
It advises verifying slot counts and character limits in the user's own ads interface or preview rather than trusting remembered numbers.
It contains no invented statistics, customers, or quotes beyond the one supplied.

evals.prompt: I'm the founder of Fernhollow, a B2B expense-audit SaaS. Before you write any ads I want your recommended messaging angles for our first paid push on a professional-network feed. Constraints from legal: we cannot name competitors, and we have zero customer quotes cleared for external use. There's no promo or renewal deadline in play. What we DO have: a measured pilot result - one customer cut duplicate-expense payouts by 31% in 90 days - approved for marketing use. Traffic will be mostly solution-aware. Results need to land before our board meeting in 3 weeks, and this is a one-off push, not an ongoing program. Give me your angle recommendation.
evals.expected_output: Ranked candidate angle sets with forbidden angles deleted and named as deleted, the outcome angle promoted because its proof asset already exists, the ranking stated out loud and tied to the deadline and one-off constraints, and an approval gate before any variant is written.
expectations: The response removes the comparison/competitor angle from the candidate set entirely, naming it as deleted due to the legal constraint, not ranked at the bottom.
It removes the social-proof/testimonial angle entirely, named as deleted because no quotes are cleared.
It removes the urgency angle, named as deleted because no real deadline or promo exists.
Each deleted angle carries its cause, so a later round re-tests the constraint rather than the angle.
It promotes the quantified-outcome angle on the grounds that the proof asset already exists and its cost is already paid.
It carries the 31% and 90-day figures through accurately, without alteration or embellishment.
It states its ranking of the remaining candidate angles explicitly in words, not implied by list order alone.
It names how the 3-week deadline moved the ranking: angles that draft the same day (such as pain) are promoted.
It accounts for solution-aware traffic by promoting mechanism/differentiator framing over opening cold on the problem alone.
It presents 2-3 candidate angle sets of roughly 3-5 angles each, with one recommendation and rationale.
It states the ranking is a default that shifts with the account's own assets and constraints, not a law.
It asks for explicit approval of an angle set before writing any full ad variants, and does not deliver finished headline/primary-text sets in this reply.
It frames the B2B copy for a reader building an internal case: the quantified outcome as a line they can defend in a meeting.

evals.prompt: Marketing lead at Quorail, a B2B fleet-telematics SaaS, average deal $14k/year, sales-led. LinkedIn ads drive demo requests - about 18 a month total. My CMO read that you should always test 3-5 ads per ad group and wants me to launch 12 copy variants next week so we 'learn faster'. We have one proven winner (a cost-savings angle) plus a driver-safety segment we've never touched. What's the play - do I write the 12?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against 12 variants at this volume, presenting the conflicting practitioner conventions as a trade-off, defaulting to 2-3 distinct angles judged on upstream signals, and spending the next slot on the untested driver-safety segment as a new variant ID.
expectations: The response recommends against launching 12 variants at this conversion volume.
It names at least two conflicting practitioner conventions on variant count (a hard cap of 3; 3-5 per ad group; a warning that 5+ dilutes traffic and inflates false positives).
It presents the trade-off - traffic dilution against hypothesis coverage - instead of endorsing one convention as settled best practice.
It states the default of about three genuinely distinct angles, and that this account's volume argues for moving down toward two, not up.
It states that B2B copy at this volume gets judged on upstream signals (CTR, lead quality) rather than conversion-level significance.
It directs the next test slot at the untested driver-safety segment, on the grounds that a proven winner plus an obvious untested segment beats the convention.
It ranks what one more slot buys: a new angle above a different awareness stage above a new formula above a new wording.
It explains that a reword costs near-zero and teaches near-zero - synonym preference, not market truth.
It treats driver-safety copy as a new variant with its own ID at V1, not a V2 of the cost-savings winner, reserving V2/V3 for wording iterations of a declared winner.
It does not compute sample size, spend, or duration, deferring test design to a separate test-planning step.
It states that the account's own testable volume decides the count, since the published conventions conflict.
Recommended angles skew to B2B arguments (quantified outcome, risk or compliance reduction, peer proof, total cost of ownership) for a reader building an internal case.
Any proposed variants are labelled with angle, awareness stage, formula, and version, or recorded in a matrix with stable IDs.

evals.prompt: Quick one. We ran 4 ad variants for Nimbleaf, our B2C houseplant subscription at $29/box. The 'free plant doctor consult' headline got 2.1% CTR vs 0.8-1.0% for the others, so it's our winner. But weirdly, conversion rate from that ad is less than half the others and CPA nearly doubled. The landing page sells the subscription box - there's no consult offer on it anywhere. Write me 8 more headlines doubling down on the free consult angle since it clearly resonates.
evals.expected_output: A response that withholds the 8 headlines, diagnoses a message-match break (the ad promises a consult the page never offers), reads the funnel top-down, and puts the page-or-angle decision to the user instead of shipping the mismatch.
expectations: The response does not deliver 8 more free-consult headlines as requested, or makes any new copy conditional on resolving the mismatch first.
It diagnoses strong CTR with weak conversion as the ad overpromising relative to the page or offer - a message-match or destination problem.
It states explicitly that this pattern is not a reason to write more headlines.
It identifies the specific mismatch: the ad promises a free consult that appears nowhere on the landing page.
It puts the decision to the user - add the consult offer to the page, or retire/adjust the angle - rather than silently shipping either way.
It reads the funnel top-down (attention, CTR, conversion rate, cost per result) and stops at the first broken gate.
It disputes calling the consult ad the winner: overpromise buys clicks that never convert.
It attributes the CTR result to the copy's promise and the conversion failure to the promise-page gap, not to bidding, audience, or tracking as the primary diagnosis.
Any replacement copy it drafts promises only what the landing page actually offers (the subscription box).
Any replacement copy is labelled with angle, awareness stage, formula, and version.
It does not produce sample-size or statistical-significance calculations for the next test.

evals.prompt: Our ad test for Threadgold (DTC bedding brand) wrapped and the reporting is a mess. In our analytics tool the same ad shows as three separate rows: 'Sleep_Cool_V1', 'sleep_cool_v1', and 'sleep-cool-v1' - the ad platform name, the tracking parameter, and the analytics label were each set by a different person. Also my teammate launched a totally new angle last week (hotel-quality luxury positioning) and named it 'sleep_cool_v2' since it was our second ad. Can you clean up how we name things before the next round?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that case and separator differences fragmented one variant into three reporting rows, a lowercase single-separator ID scheme mirrored across every tracking surface, the luxury angle re-labelled as a new ID at V1, and a variant matrix with hypothesis and evidence columns.
expectations: The response diagnoses the three-row split as caused by case and separator differences in the tracked values - the analytics tool treats differently-cased values as separate rows.
It prescribes one identical identifier mirrored across the ad name, the tracking parameter, and the analytics label.
It prescribes all-lowercase values with one consistent separator.
It separates the stable ID from the human-readable name, so renaming never breaks tracking history.
It proposes an ID scheme encoding angle, awareness stage, sequence, and version (e.g. angle_awareness_seq_vN).
It corrects the 'sleep_cool_v2' label: the luxury positioning is a new angle and gets its own new ID at V1, not a V2 of the old ad.
It states that V2/V3 markers are reserved for wording iterations of the same angle after it wins.
It recommends that one person approve any new tracking value before launch.
It recommends recording the set in a variant matrix, one row per variant, including a one-line hypothesis per variant.
The matrix includes an evidence-source column tracing each proof point to user-supplied material.
It states that a matrix without version codes or tracking mapping is incomplete.
It keeps the naming and tracking glossary (separator, casing, codes) with the matrix rather than in a separate document.

evals.prompt: Write ad copy for Peakform, our B2C posture-trainer wearable at $79. Two placements: LinkedIn feed and Instagram feed - you know the character limits, just use those. The target audience has never heard of posture trainers as a category; most don't even connect their back pain to sitting posture. I want the product name front and center in every headline since we're building the brand, plus a few emojis to pop. We have 60 Trustpilot reviews I can paste if useful.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to trust remembered character limits and asks for the user's current ones, opens on the symptom rather than the product name for unaware traffic, flags emoji counting and health-implying phrasing, asks for the reviews, and schedules a humanizing pass with a length re-check.
expectations: The response does not assert platform character limits from memory as authoritative; it asks the user to paste current limits from their ads manager or states that remembered limits go stale.
It states that the user's own ad preview is the final authority on fit.
It warns that the professional-network placement clips headlines permanently with no expander, or asks the user to confirm truncation behaviour per placement.
It plans the key phrase to land before the fold or clip point on each placement.
It warns that emojis can count as more than one character.
It pushes back on leading every headline with the product name, explaining that naming the product first to an unaware reader is wasted.
It opens unaware-stage copy on the symptom or an arresting truth (e.g. the sitting-posture connection) rather than on the product.
It avoids or flags second-person phrasing that asserts the reader has back pain, as implying knowledge of a health condition.
It asks for the 60 Trustpilot reviews, or conditions any proof line on receiving them.
Any drafted copy contains no fabricated review quotes, ratings, or statistics.
It includes a humanizing pass over headlines, primary text, and descriptions before final delivery, rather than shipping raw first-draft output.
It re-checks surface fit after the humanizing pass because lengths change.
In drafted variants, the headline complements the primary text rather than repeating it.
